title: Preventing SQL Injection in Java JDBC and JPA/Hibernate
content: In Java JDBC, building SQL strings with string concatenation (+ operators or StringBuilder) exposes applications to SQL injection. Using java.sql.PreparedStatement ensures SQL syntax and user data are separated at the database engine level. In JPA/Hibernate, always use named parameter binding.
remediation_guidelines: Always use java.sql.PreparedStatement with parameter index placeholders (?).
In JPA/Hibernate, use named parameters (:param) instead of string concatenation in JPQL/HQL queries.

title: Preventing Path Traversal in Java File I/O
content: Accepting unvalidated filenames in Java File or java.nio.file.Path constructors allows directory traversal sequences (../ or ..\) to access files outside the intended root directory. Validating the canonical path or using Path.normalize() and startsWith() prevents path traversal.
vulnerable_example:
File file = new File("/var/uploads/" + request.getParameter("filename"));
FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream(file);
remediation_guidelines: Normalize and resolve paths against a safe root directory using java.nio.file.Path.
Check that the resolved path startsWith() the normalized base directory.
Never trust raw filenames supplied by clients without sanitization.

title: Safe Deserialization in Java and ObjectInputFilter
content: Java standard serialization via java.io.ObjectInputStream allows arbitrary object graphs to be deserialized, triggering gadget chains (e.g. Apache Commons Collections) that lead to remote arbitrary code execution. Migrating to JSON (Jackson) or applying ObjectInputFilter whitelists is required.
vulnerable_example:
ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(clientSocket.getInputStream());
Object obj = ois.readObject(); // Vulnerable to gadget chains
remediation_guidelines: Avoid ObjectInputStream whenever possible; use JSON, Protobuf, or XML with safe parsers.
If native Java serialization is required, implement an ObjectInputFilter allowlist.

title: Declarative Method-Level Access Control & IDOR in Spring
content: Relying purely on URL route patterns in HttpSecurity leaves controller methods vulnerable to authorization bypass and Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR). Using Spring Security @PreAuthorize ensures resource ownership is validated at the method invocation level.
remediation_guidelines: Annotate sensitive endpoints with @PreAuthorize expressions verifying ownership.
Never expose database sequential IDs without checking user tenancy.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Defense in Java HTTP Clients
content: Calling URL.openStream() or HttpClient.send() with unvalidated URLs allows attackers to target internal IP spaces, cloud instance metadata services (169.254.169.254), and local management ports.
vulnerable_example:
URL url = new URL(userProvidedUrl);
InputStream in = url.openStream();
remediation_guidelines: Resolve DNS and verify that IP addresses do not fall within private (RFC 1918) or loopback ranges.
Whitelist allowed outbound domain names and protocols (strictly https).

title: Spring Security CORS & CSRF Hardening
content: Configuring Spring Security with allowedOrigins('*') and allowCredentials(true) allows unauthorized origins to read sensitive data and make cross-site authenticated requests. Disabling CSRF in cookie-authenticated web sessions exposes users to CSRF attacks.
remediation_guidelines: Explicitly list approved origin URLs in CORS configuration.
Enable CookieCsrfTokenRepository for stateful session-based web applications.

title: Preventing Stack Trace & Information Disclosure in Spring Boot
content: Default Spring Boot error controllers display full class names, stack traces, and framework versions upon runtime exceptions. Actuator endpoints exposed to the public internet leak environment variables, JVM memory metrics, and heap dumps.
vulnerable_example:
# application.properties with debug error messages
server.error.include-stacktrace=always
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*
secure_example:
# Hardened application.properties
server.error.include-stacktrace=never
server.error.include-message=never
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
remediation_guidelines: Set server.error.include-stacktrace=never in production.
Restrict Spring Actuator web endpoint exposure to authenticated admin networks.

title: Supply Chain Security & Maven Dependency-Check Integration
content: Java applications rely on extensive Maven/Gradle dependency trees. Vulnerable libraries (such as unpatched Log4j, Spring Framework, or SnakeYAML) introduce remote code execution risks.
vulnerable_example:
<!-- Unaudited pom.xml dependencies with known CVEs -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>log4j-core</artifactId>
    <version>2.14.1</version>
</dependency>
secure_example:
<!-- OWASP Dependency-Check Maven plugin with build break gate -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
    <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
    <version>9.0.9</version>
    <configuration><failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS></configuration>
    <executions><execution><goals><goal>check</goal></goals></execution></executions>
</plugin>
remediation_guidelines: Incorporate owasp:dependency-check-maven into CI/CD build pipelines.
Establish automated dependency update policies via Dependabot or Renovate.

title: Password Hashing with BCryptPasswordEncoder & Argon2
content: Using java.security.MessageDigest with MD5, SHA-1, or plain SHA-256 lacks computational cost and salt protection against rainbow table lookups and GPU brute-forcing.
vulnerable_example:
MessageDigest md = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5");
byte[] digest = md.digest(password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
remediation_guidelines: Use Spring Security's BCryptPasswordEncoder or Argon2PasswordEncoder.
Never use fast hashing algorithms for credentials.

title: Cryptographic Randomness with SecureRandom
content: java.util.Random utilizes a linear congruential formula that is easily predictable from previous outputs. Security tokens, CSRF tokens, and session keys require java.security.SecureRandom.
vulnerable_example:
Random random = new Random();
int token = random.nextInt(1000000);
remediation_guidelines: Use SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong() for all cryptographic key and token generation.
Avoid java.util.Random for any security-sensitive operations.

title: Authenticated Encryption with AES-256-GCM
content: Encrypting data with AES in ECB mode leaks structural patterns, and CBC mode without authentication is vulnerable to bit-flipping and padding oracle attacks. AES-GCM provides both confidentiality and message integrity.
vulnerable_example:
Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding");
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey);
remediation_guidelines: Use AES/GCM/NoPadding with 128-bit authentication tag and 96-bit unique IV.
Never reuse an IV under the same secret key.

title: OS Command Injection Prevention with ProcessBuilder
content: Using Runtime.getRuntime().exec("sh -c " + cmd) passes user input directly to the operating system shell, allowing command separators like &&, |, and ; to execute arbitrary shell scripts.
vulnerable_example: Runtime.getRuntime().exec("ping -c 1 " + hostName);
remediation_guidelines: Use ProcessBuilder with arguments supplied in separate array strings.
Perform regex validation on arguments before invoking external executables.

title: XML External Entity (XXE) Prevention in Java Parsers
content: Java standard XML factories (DocumentBuilderFactory, SAXParserFactory, XMLInputFactory) resolve external entities by default, allowing attackers to access local server files (/etc/passwd, win.ini) and internal cloud services.
vulnerable_example:
DocumentBuilderFactory dbf = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
Document doc = dbf.newDocumentBuilder().parse(inputStream);
remediation_guidelines: Set disallow-doctype-decl to true on all DocumentBuilderFactory instances.
Disable external-general-entities and external-parameter-entities.

title: LDAP Injection Defense in JNDI Lookups
content: Concatenating user inputs into LDAP search filter strings allows attackers to alter query logic, retrieve hidden attributes, or bypass corporate authentication filters.
vulnerable_example:
String filter = "(&(uid=" + username + ")(userPassword=" + pass + "))";
NamingEnumeration<SearchResult> results = ctx.search("ou=users", filter, controls);
secure_example:
String filter = "(&(uid={0})(userPassword={1}))";
NamingEnumeration<SearchResult> results = ctx.search("ou=users", filter, new Object[]{username, pass}, controls);
remediation_guidelines: Use parameterized search methods in InitialDirContext.
Sanitize special LDAP characters (*, (, ), \, NUL) if manual filtering is required.

title: Rate Limiting in Spring Boot with Bucket4j
content: Unprotected login and sensitive API endpoints allow rapid automated credential stuffing and denial of service. Integrating token-bucket rate limiting via Bucket4j restricts request velocity.
remediation_guidelines: Deploy rate-limiting filters on authentication and password reset routes.
Use Redis-backed distributed token buckets for clustered deployments.

title: Externalizing Credentials via Spring @Value and Vault
content: Hardcoding API secrets, encryption keys, and database passwords in Java source files or unencrypted application.properties causes credential exposure in source code repositories.
vulnerable_example: private static final String API_KEY = "sk-live-12345abcdef67890";
remediation_guidelines: Inject secrets via environment variables or Spring Cloud Vault.
Never commit production credentials to version control.

title: Secure JWT Validation with JJWT / Nimbus
content: Decoding JWT tokens without verifying the cryptographic signature or allowing unsigned alg: none tokens enables authentication bypass. Symmetric HMAC signing (HS256) requires high-entropy secrets (>= 256 bits) and strict algorithm allowlisting to prevent algorithm-confusion attacks. Externalize secrets using a dedicated secrets manager and rotate exposed secrets immediately. For distributed microservice architectures where multiple services verify tokens without sharing the private signing key, migrate to asymmetric public/private keys (RS256 or ES256).
vulnerable_example: Claims claims = Jwts.parser().parseClaimsJwt(token).getBody();
remediation_guidelines: Always call parseClaimsJws() with a verified signing key and enforce explicit algorithm allowlists.
Ensure symmetric HMAC secrets have at least 256 bits of entropy and are stored in a secrets manager.
For distributed token verification, use asymmetric key pairs (RS256/ES256).
Rotate signing secrets immediately if credentials have been exposed.

title: Preventing CRLF Log Injection and Credential Leakage in SLF4J
content: Logging unsanitized user inputs containing carriage returns (\r) and line feeds (\n) allows log forging, tricking SOC analysts or corrupting SIEM log parsers. Logging passwords or session IDs breaches compliance.
vulnerable_example: logger.info("Login attempt for user: " + username + " with password: " + password);
secure_example:
String cleanUsername = username.replaceAll("[\r\n]", "_");
logger.warn("Authentication failed for user: {}", cleanUsername);
remediation_guidelines: Sanitize newlines from user inputs before writing to logs.
Mask passwords and tokens using Logback custom pattern converters.

title: Eliminating Empty Catch Blocks and InterruptedException Suppression
content: Empty catch blocks silently swallow exceptions, hiding system crashes and leaving the application in an indeterminate state. Suppressing InterruptedException prevents worker threads from shutting down cleanly.
remediation_guidelines: Never leave catch blocks empty; log the exception with full diagnostic stack traces.
If catching InterruptedException, restore the interrupted status with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

title: Resource Leak Prevention with Try-With-Resources
content: Failing to close database connections, sockets, and file streams leads to file descriptor exhaustion and database connection pool starvation under production loads. Using Java 7+ try-with-resources guarantees automatic resource closure.
remediation_guidelines: Implement AutoCloseable for all stateful resources.
Always manage I/O and JDBC streams with try-with-resources blocks.

title: Declaring Specific Exception Types Instead of Generic throws Exception
content: Declaring 'throws Exception' in Java method signatures violates exception abstraction, obscures failure modes from callers, forces callers to catch generic java.lang.Exception, and defeats Java checked exception system. Methods must declare specific checked exception types (such as NoSuchAlgorithmException, GeneralSecurityException, IOException, SQLException) based on the exact operations performed, or catch low-level checked exceptions internally and wrap them in descriptive, domain-specific exceptions.
remediation_guidelines: Replace 'throws Exception' with the specific checked exception types thrown by called APIs (e.g. GeneralSecurityException, IOException, SQLException).
Catch checked exceptions internally and wrap them into descriptive runtime or domain exceptions when appropriate.
Never declare generic 'throws Exception' or 'throws Throwable' on public service interfaces.
